source_text: Certe Apostolus est, et praecipua Domino Iesu caritate dilectus; tamen nisi intentionem eius, vel Evangelium quod scripsit, vel Epistolarum gravitas indicaret, verba ista quae posuimus, ita nullum possent rebus afferre praeiudicium, ut Scripturis omnibus, quae mundum a Deo factum asserunt, cedere cogerentur. Verum ipse Evangelii quod conscripsit, reverendo se communivit exordio. Deus - inquit - erat Verbum; per ipsum facta sunt omnia, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Ac deinceps: Erat lumen verum, quod illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum; in hoc mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est. Itemque: Verbum caro factum est, ut habitaret in nobis [n35] . Quibus testimoniis nihil in sensibus suis obscuritatis reliquit; sed ostendit Deum se nosse et asserere totius mundi, atque eorum quae in mundo sunt omnium conditorem, Manichaeisque nullum ad sententias suas accessum patere perdocuit. Quoniam qui omnium naturarum Deum asserit creatorem, abutitur, sine fidei dispendio, substantiarum nominibus, ad significationem cupiditatis immodicae.
pass_a_gloss: He is certainly the Apostle, and loved with especial charity by the Lord Jesus; nevertheless unless his intention were indicated either by the Gospel which he wrote or by the gravity of the Letters, those words which we have set down could so little bring a prior judgment against the facts that they would be compelled to yield to all the Scriptures which assert that the world was made by God. But he fortified himself by the reverend beginning of the Gospel which he composed. God — he says — was the Word; through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made. And next: He was the true light, which illuminates every human being coming into this world; he was in this world, and the world was made through him. And likewise: The Word was made flesh, that he might dwell in us. By which testimonies he left nothing of obscurity in his senses; but he showed that he knows and asserts God as founder of the whole world and of all things which are in the world, and he thoroughly taught that no access lies open to the Manichaeans through his sentences. Because he who asserts God the creator of all natures misuses, without loss of faith, the names of substances for the signification of immoderate desire.

pass_b_english: He is certainly an apostle, loved by the Lord Jesus with a special affection (compare John 13:23). Yet if neither the Gospel he wrote nor the weight of his letters revealed his intention, these words I have quoted could count in no way against created things: they would have to give way to all the Scriptures that declare the world was made by God. But he himself secured his position in the revered opening of the Gospel he wrote. “The Word,” he says, “was God. Everything was made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1, 3) (John 13:23). And afterward: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world. He was in this world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:9–10). Again: “The Word became flesh, to dwell among us” (John 1:14). These testimonies leave no obscurity in his meaning. They show that he knows and proclaims God as creator of the whole world and of everything in it, and thoroughly demonstrate that the Manichaeans have no way into his teaching. For someone who proclaims God as creator of all natures can use the names of substances figuratively to signify excessive desire, without damage to the faith.
